\section{Introduction}

\subsection{SLAM Literature Review}\label{sub:Literature Review} % (fold)
    Active simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is the problem of controlling
    a robot in an effort toward both accurately estimating its pose
    and constructing a map of its environment \cite{placed2023active}.
    The necessity for simultaneous operations is driven by applications where
    pre-mapping is infeasible due to dynamic environments, resource
    constraints, or inaccessible locations such as underwater, underground, or
    extraterrestrial exploration \cite{stachniss2009robotic}. Although most
    research focuses on estimation, active SLAM techniques have been shown to
    significantly improve exploration efficiency and reduce mapping uncertainty
    \cite{placed2023active,sim2005active}.

    Early SLAM approaches relied on extended Kalman filters (EKF), which
    by assuming locally linear and Gaussian dynamics maintain a Gaussian belief
    over the current robot pose and map, updating the belief recursively as new
    measurements arrive \cite{smith1990estimating}. EKF-based SLAM suffers from
    inconsistency over long trajectories: linearization errors accumulate,
    producing overly optimistic covariance estimates that fail to reflect true
    uncertainty \cite{bailey2006consistency,huang2007convergence}.
    Additionally, the requirement to maintain a full covariance matrix over all
    landmarks scales quadratically with map size, limiting applicability to
    environments with few features.

    % Particle filter approaches
    Rao-Blackwellized particle filters (RBPF) \cite{Murphy2001}, exemplified by
    FastSLAM \cite[Chapter~13]{thrun2005probabilistic}, addressed computational scaling by
    representing the robot trajectory with particles while marginalizing
    landmarks analytically via per-particle Kalman filters. This factorization
    reduces the effective dimensionality from the full state (trajectory plus
    all landmarks) to just the trajectory. However, particle filters face
    consistency issues of their own \cite{bailey2006consistencya} as well as
    the issue of particle degeneracy (after repeated resampling, all particles
    collapse to a few trajectories) and require exponentially many samples to
    accurately represent high-dimensional distributions
    \cite{barfoot2024state}, limiting their reliability for extended operation.

    % Factor graph SLAM 
    Graph-based SLAM methods reformulate the problem as \textit{maximum a
    posteriori} (MAP) estimation over the full robot trajectory and map,
    representing the posterior as a factor graph where nodes correspond to
    variables (poses, landmarks) and edges encode probabilistic constraints
    from motion and sensor models \cite{thrun2006graphslam}. Unlike
    filtering approaches that maintain only the current belief state, these
    batch methods solve for the entire history jointly by minimizing a
    nonlinear least squares objective via iterative optimization
    \cite{barfoot2024state}. This naturally handles loop closures and avoids
    filter inconsistency by relinearizing around updated estimates after
    incorporating all available data, rather than suffering from accumulated
    linearization errors. However, early batch implementations solve the full
    optimization problem at each time-step, recomputing matrix factorizations
    from scratch \cite{dellaert2006square}. While exploiting sparsity via
    variable ordering reduced complexity substantially, repeatedly computing
    the full solution remained computationally expensive for real-time
    operation.
    
    Incremental methods have enabled real-time batch optimization by reusing
    prior computation. iSAM \cite{kaess2008isam} stored the square root
    information matrix and incrementally updated only affected entries when new
    measurements arrived, though loop closures necessitate expensive periodic
    reordering. iSAM2 \cite{kaess2012isam2} eliminated batch reordering via the
    Bayes tree (a data structure encoding conditional independence) and
    introduced fluid relinearization, updating only variables whose estimates
    changed significantly. These advances form the foundation of modern
    optimization libraries like GTSAM \cite{gtsam}. For long-term autonomy,
    fixed-lag smoothing \cite{dong2012consistency} bounds computational cost by
    marginalizing old states outside a sliding window, though marginalization
    destroys sparsity \cite{eustice2006exactly}. Hierarchical systems like
    ORB-SLAM \cite{mur2015orb} instead schedule computation at multiple
    granularities: fast motion-only tracking, bounded local bundle adjustment,
    and infrequent global pose graph optimization. While sacrificing the global
    optimality of full batch methods, these approaches achieve real-time
    performance in large-scale environments.

    %% Invariant EKF
    Concurrently with batch method developments, invariant extended Kalman
    filters (IEKFs) emerged to address the consistency issues plaguing
    classical EKF-SLAM while preserving the computational efficiency of
    filtering \cite{barrau2017invariant}. Julier and Uhlmann
    \cite{julier2001counter} first demonstrated through a counterexample that
    EKF-SLAM produces inconsistent estimates when the robot is stationary, with
    the robot orientation uncertainty being identified as the key culprit.
    Huang and Dissanayake \cite{huang2007convergence} proved that EKF-SLAM
    incorrectly reduces robot orientation uncertainty when observing new
    landmarks (i.e., with unknown absolute locations), violating results
    \cite[Corollary~3.3,3.6]{huang2007convergence} showing that such
    observations cannot reduce robot pose uncertainty. The root cause is that
    linearization errors accumulate in a way that causes the filter to believe
    it has more information about the robot's orientation than is actually
    available from the measurements.

    By exploiting the Lie group structure of the state space (e.g., $SE(3)$ for
    rigid body pose), IEKFs perform linearization in coordinates where
    unobservable directions (such as global rotation) become independent of the
    linearization point. This ensures the filter's uncertainty representation
    remains consistent with the true unobservabilities of the SLAM problem. The
    resulting filters maintain quadratic computational scaling with map size
    achieving markedly improved consistency over long trajectories. Barrau and
    Bonnabel \cite{barrau2015iekf,barrau2018iekf} proved that IEKF-SLAM
    maintains correct observability properties and demonstrated this
    experimentally on the Victoria Park dataset. Subsequent work extended this
    framework to visual-inertial SLAM, with \cite{brossard2018invariant}
    showing that unscented Kalman filters on Lie groups (UKF-LG)
    \cite{brossard2017ukflg} offer similar performance to IEKFs with simpler
    implementation and reduced computational cost. The Gaussian assumption
    remains pervasive across both filtering and batch approaches (save for
    particle filtering), limiting applicability when measurement distributions
    are heavy-tailed or when data association is ambiguous, yielding multimodal
    posteriors that Gaussian representations cannot capture.

    The geometric foundations underlying these invariant filtering approaches
    were further developed by Mahony and Hamel \cite{mahony2017geometric}, who
    formulated the SLAM state space as a quotient manifold $\mathcal{M}_n(3)$
    under reference frame transformations and introduced the $\text{SLAM}_n(3)$
    symmetry group whose transitive action yields equivariant kinematics.
    Working in the deterministic observer framework rather than stochastic
    filtering, they designed nonlinear observers with provable exponential
    convergence via Lyapunov analysis.
    
    
    By formulating active SLAM as a partially observable Markov decision process
    (POMDP), stochastic control techniques have been applied with some success. 
    Much work has focused on the related problem of belief-space planning
    (BSP), which encompasses path planning under uncertainty, active
    localization, and exploration as special cases \cite{indelman2015planning}.
    However, most BSP approaches rely on Gaussian belief
    representations and local optimization
    without global convergence guarantees
    \cite{platt2010belief,van2012motion,indelman2015planning}.
    Extensions imposing belief uncertainty constraints \cite{rahman2021uncertainty}
    were adapted to active SLAM in \cite{koga2022active}.
    Information-theoretic metrics have proven effective as
    utility functions for active SLAM, particularly \emph{information gain}
    \cite{stachniss2009robotic} and variants based on R\'enyi entropy
    \cite{carrillo2018autonomous} and generalized behavioral entropy
    \cite{suresh2024behave}. A mutual information-based metric was shown to
    provably steer robots toward unexplored areas
    \cite{julian2013mutual}.

    Recently, rigorous approximation and learning methods for POMDPs in general
    state and action spaces have been developed. Saldi et al.
    \cite{saldi2019asymptotic} showed that quantization-based finite models
    yield near-optimal policies under weak continuity conditions.
    Subsequent work on finite memory approximations and Q-learning convergence
    for both schemes is surveyed in \cite{kara2024pomdp}.

\section{Preliminaries}\label{sec:Preliminaries} % (fold)
In this section, we introduce the general components typical of active SLAM and
related BSP problems, specifically covering the motion model, representation of
the map, and sensor model.

Let $(\mathcal{W}, d_{\mathcal{W}})$ be a compact
Euclidean metric space representing the workspace of the robot, equipped with
the Euclidean metric $d_{\mathcal{W}}(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ and the Lebesgue measure
$\lambda$ restricted to $\mathcal{W}$.
    \subsection{Motion model}\label{sec:Motion model} % (fold)
    Let $\mathbb{X}$ be a standard Borel space (i.e., a Borel space associated with a complete separable metric space) that denotes the set of all
    possible poses of the robot. Let $x_{t}\in \mathbb{X}$ denote
    the pose of the robot at $t\ge 0$. The robot pose evolves in time according
    to a controlled stochastic process
    \begin{equation} 
        x_{t+1} = f(x_t, u_t, \xi_t), \quad \xi_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mu_\xi,
        \label{eq:robot_dynamics} 
    \end{equation}
    where $u_t \in \mathbb{U}$ is the control input and $\xi_t\in \mathbb{R}^d,d>1$
    represents an independent and identically distributed (iid) process noise
    with distribution $\mu_{\xi}$ (written as $\xi_{t}\stackrel{\text{iid}}\sim
    \mu_\xi$).
    Examples for $f$ include the following.
    \begin{example}[Unicycle dynamics \cite{salzmann2020trajectron++,martinelli2015complete}]
        Setting $s_t = (x_{t}, y_{t}, \theta_t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \times S^1$ 
        (with $S^1$ denoting the circle group), $u_t =
        (a_t, \omega_t)$, and $\xi_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$ (where $\mathbf{I}$ is the $2\times2$ identity matrix), we have $s_{t+1} = f(s_{t},u_{t},\xi_{t})$ or
        \begin{equation*}
            \begin{pmatrix}
                x_{t+1}\\ y_{t+1}\\ v_{t}\\ \theta_{t}
            \end{pmatrix}
            \!\!\!=\!\!\!
            \begin{pmatrix}
                x_{t}+\cos(\theta_{t})v_{t}\Delta t\\
                y_{t}+\sin(\theta_{t})v_{t}\Delta t\\
                v_{t}+a_{t}\Delta t\\
                \theta_{t}+\omega_{t}\Delta t
            \end{pmatrix}
            \!+\!
            \begin{pmatrix}
                0 & 0\\
                0 & 0\\
                \sqrt{K_{v}} & 0\\
                0 & \sqrt{K_{\theta}}
            \end{pmatrix}\!\!\sqrt{|v_{t}|\Delta t}\xi_{t},
        \end{equation*}
        with $\Delta t>0$ denoting the time step and parameters $K_{v},K_{\theta}$ characterizing our system. 
    \end{example}
    \begin{example}[Dubins airplane \cite{chitsaz2007time}]
        Setting $s_t = (x_t, y_t, z_t, \theta_t) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \times S^1$,
        $u_t = (u_{z,t}, u_{\theta,t})$, and $\xi_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})$, we have
        \begin{align*}
            s_{t+1} &= f(s_t, u_t, \xi_t), \\
            \begin{pmatrix}
                x_{t+1} \\ y_{t+1} \\ z_{t+1} \\ \theta_{t+1}
            \end{pmatrix} &= \begin{pmatrix}
                x_t + v \cos(\theta_t) \Delta t \\
                y_t + v \sin(\theta_t) \Delta t \\
                z_t + u_{z,t} \Delta t \\
                \theta_t + u_{\theta,t} \Delta t
            \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}
                0 & 0 \\
                0 & 0 \\
                \sigma_z  & 0 \\
                0 & \sigma_\theta 
            \end{pmatrix} \sqrt{\Delta t}\xi_t,
        \end{align*}
        with constant forward speed $v$, altitude rate $u_z$, turn rate $u_\theta$,
        and noise parameters $\sigma_z, \sigma_\theta$.
    \end{example}
    % subsection Motion model (end)

    \subsection{Modelling the map}\label{sub:Modelling the map} % (fold)
    Let $\mathbb{M}$ be a standard Borel space representing the space of maps. The representation of the map varies across different approaches in SLAM, this formulation subsumes these various representations including occupancy maps and landmark-based maps. 
    
    \textbf{Occupancy maps} are represented by an occupied
    region $m\subseteq \mathcal{W}$. We define the map space as the
    family of nonempty compact subsets:
    \begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{M}_{\text{occ}} := \{ m\subseteq \mathcal{W}: m \text{
    compact}, m \ne \emptyset
    \}. 
    \end{equation*}
    Equipped with the Hausdorff metric $d_H$ (or other variants introduced in
    \cite{baddeley1992errors}), $\mathbb{M}_{\text{occ}}$ is a compact metric
    space whenever $\mathcal{W}$ is compact
    \cite{fell1962hausdorff,baddeley1992errors}.    

    \textbf{Landmark-based maps} are defined as a finite collection of locations corresponding 
    to landmarks. The map space is defined as   
    $\mathbb{M}_{\ell}\coloneq \mathcal{W}^{ \overline{\ell }}$
    equipped with the Euclidean metric (assuming perfect
    data association and labelled landmarks), where $\overline{\ell }>0$
    represents the number of landmarks.

    The metric space structure of the map is critical in establishing (i)
    continuity properties of the dynamics and observations,
    (ii) continuity of the stage cost, and (iii) compactness properties. 
    
    Let $m_{t}$ denote the state of the map at time $t\ge 0$. The map $m_t$ is
    assumed to be static, so its dynamics are simply described as
    \begin{equation}
        m_{t+1} = m_t,\quad t\ge 0.
        \label{eq:map dynamics}
    \end{equation}
    % subsection Modelling the map (end)

    \subsection{Sensor model}\label{sub:Sensor model} % (fold)
    Let $\mathbb{Y}$ be a standard Borel space that denotes the observation space. 
    At each time step $t\ge0$, the robot receives noisy observations
    $y_t \in \mathbb{Y}$ of the environment according to a measurement model 
    \begin{equation} 
        y_t = g(x_{t}, m_{t}, u_{t-1}, \zeta_t), \quad \zeta_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mu_{\zeta},
        \label{eq:measurement_model} 
    \end{equation}
    where $\zeta_t\in \mathbb{R}^d,d>0$.
    The measurement dynamics stated generally in \eqref{eq:measurement_model}
    vary across sensor modalities. Following the general classification of
    \cite[Chapter~1.2]{barfoot2024state}, robotic sensors
    can be divided into two distinct categories: proprioceptive and exteroceptive.
    
    \textbf{Proprioceptive sensors} measure internal robotic state, are 
    control-dependent, and are independent of the map: $y_t^{\text{prop}} = 
    g^{\text{prop}}(x_t, u_{t-1},v_t)$ \cite[Section~7.4.4]{barfoot2024state}. 
    Examples of proprioceptive sensors include inertial measurement units
    (IMU), gyroscopes, wheel encoders, and joint encoders. 
    \begin{example}[IMU \cite{burnett2025imu}]
        State $s_{t}=(p_{t}, v_{t}, a_{t}, \omega_{t}, b_{a,t}, b_{\omega,t})$ includes pose,
        body-frame velocities $(v_t, \omega_t)$, body-frame acceleration $a_t$, and biases $(b_{a,t},b_{\omega,t})$.
        IMU measurement model with $\zeta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R})$ (up to a coordinate transform):
        \begin{align*}
            y_t^{\text{imu}} = \begin{bmatrix} \tilde{a}_t \\ \tilde{\omega}_t \end{bmatrix}
            &= \begin{bmatrix} a_t - \mathbf{g}_t \\ \omega_t \end{bmatrix}
            + \begin{bmatrix} b_{a,t} \\ b_{\omega,t} \end{bmatrix}
            + \begin{bmatrix} \zeta_t^a \\ \zeta_t^\omega \end{bmatrix},
        \end{align*}
        where $\mathbf{g}_t$ is gravity expressed in sensor frame. Accelerometer measures
        specific force (acceleration minus gravity); gyroscope directly measures angular velocity,
        both corrupted by slowly-drifting biases and white noise.
    \end{example}

    \textbf{Exteroceptive sensors} measure the state of the external environment 
    and, in contrast to proprioceptive sensors, are independent of the 
    control and a function of the map: $y_t^{\text{ext}} = 
    g^{\text{ext}}(x_t, m_t, \zeta_t)$ \cite[Section~7.4]{barfoot2024state}. 
    Examples of exteroceptive sensors include LIDAR, sonar, and cameras.
    \begin{example}[2D LIDAR]
        State $s_t = (x_t, y_t, \theta_t)$ is the robot pose; map $m \in \mathbb{M}_{\text{occ}}$ 
        is the occupied region. LIDAR with $K>0$ beams at angles $\{\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_K\}$ 
        relative to robot frame measure range to obstacles:
        \begin{align*}
            y_t^{\text{lidar}} &= \begin{bmatrix} r_1 \\ \vdots \\ r_K \end{bmatrix} 
            = \begin{bmatrix} h_1(s_t, m) \\ \vdots \\ h_K(s_t, m) \end{bmatrix} 
            + \begin{bmatrix} \zeta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \zeta_K \end{bmatrix},
        \end{align*}
        where $\zeta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_r^2)$ is range noise. For beam $i$, 
        let $\mathbf{d}_i = (\cos(\theta_t + \phi_i), \sin(\theta_t + \phi_i))$ 
        be the unit direction vector. Then
        \begin{equation*}
            h_i(s_t, m) = \inf\left\{\tau \geq 0 : (x_t, y_t) + \tau \mathbf{d}_i \in m\right\}
        \end{equation*}
        is the distance along ray $i$ to the first occupied point in $m$.
    \end{example}

    appropriate dependence structure.

\section{SLAM as a nonstandard POMDP}\label{sec:SLAM as a nonstandard POMDP} % (fold)
    We formulate active SLAM as a nonstandard POMDP over the joint state space $\mathbb{S} =
    \mathbb{X} \times \mathbb{M}$, where $s_{t}=(x_{t},m_{t})\in \mathbb{S}$,
    by describing the dynamics and observations through stochastic kernels.

    Let $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{X})$ be the set of probability measures on
    $\mathbb{X}$ endowed with the weak convergence topology. The pose dynamics
    \eqref{eq:robot_dynamics} induce a transition kernel $\mathcal{T}:
    \mathbb{X} \times \mathbb{U} \to \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{X})$ 
    defined by
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{P}(x_{t+1}\in\cdot\mid x_t=x,\, u_t=u)&= \mu_{\xi}(\{\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d : f(x, u, \xi)\in \cdot\,\}) \nonumber\\
        &\coloneqq\mathcal{T}(\, \cdot \mid x,u).
        \label{eq:pose_kernel}
    \end{align}
    The map dynamics are trivially given by the Dirac measure
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbb{P}(m_{t+1} \in \cdot \mid m_t)\coloneqq \delta_{m_t}(\,\cdot\,)
        =\begin{cases}
            1&\text{if }m_{t+1}=m_t\\0&\text{otherwise.}
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    The observation kernel $\mathcal{O}: \mathbb{S}\times\mathbb{U} \to
    \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Y})$ induced by \eqref{eq:measurement_model} is
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{P}(y_t\in\cdot\mid s_t=s,u_t=u)&=\nonumber\mu_{\zeta}(\{\zeta \in \mathbb{R}^d : g(s,u, \zeta) \in \cdot\,\})\\
        & \coloneqq\mathcal{O}(\,\cdot \mid s,u).
        \label{eq:observation_kernel}
    \end{align}
    We define active SLAM as a nonstandard $\rho$-POMDP \cite{araya2010pomdp},
    described by $(\mathbb{S}, \mathbb{U}, \mathbb{Y},
    \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{O}, \rho, \beta)$,
    with state
    transition kernel, 
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{S}(B_x \times B_m \mid (x_t, m_t), u_t) = 
        \mathcal{T}(B_x \mid x_t, u_t) \delta_{m_t}(B_m)
        \label{eq:augmented_transition}
    \end{equation}
    for sets $B_x \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{X})$ and $B_m \in
    \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{M})$, where $\mathcal{B}(\,\cdot\,)$ denotes the Borel
    $\sigma$-algebra, $\rho:\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S}) \times \mathbb{U} \to
    \mathbb{R}$ is a stage cost dependent on some probability distribution, and
    $\beta \in (0,1)$ is the discount factor.
    The nonstandard aspect of this formulation comes from the fact that the stage cost $\rho$ is dependent on the belief rather than the hidden state as would be the case in a standard POMDP formulation.

    \subsection{Belief MDP Reformulation}\label{sub:belief_mdp}
    Since the hidden state $s_{t}$ is not directly observable, decision-making 
    conditions on the posterior probability distribution of $s_{t}$, commonly
    referred to as the \emph{belief}, denoted by $b_{t}\in
    \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})$
    \begin{equation}
        b_{t}(\,\cdot \,)\coloneq \mathbb{P}(s_{t}\in \cdot \mid y_{[0,t]},u_{[0,t-1]})
        \label{eq:belief}
    \end{equation}
    where $\mathbb{B}\coloneq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})$ is the belief space.
    The belief evolves via the nonlinear filter
    $\mathbf{F}:\mathbb{B}\times\mathbb{U}\times\mathbb{Y}\to\mathbb{B}$,
    \begin{align}
        b_{t+1}
        &\coloneq \mathbf{F}(b,u,y)\nonumber\\
        &= \mathbb{P}(s_{t+1}\in\cdot\mid b_t=b,\, u_t=u,\, y_{t+1}=y).
        \label{eq:belief_update}
    \end{align}
    Suppose the observation kernel $\mathcal{O}$ is dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\lambda$ on $\mathbb{Y}$, i.e., $\mathcal{O}(\cdot\mid s)\ll \lambda$ for every $s\in\mathbb{S}$, and define the likelihood function $o(s,y)\coloneq\frac{d\mathcal{O}(\cdot\mid s)}{d\lambda}(y)$.
    Then, writing $s'=(x',m')$ and using \eqref{eq:augmented_transition},
    \begin{equation}
        b_{t+1}(ds')
        \!=\! \frac{\int_{\mathbb{X}}o(s',y_{t+1})
        \mathcal{T}(dx'\mid x,u_t)\,b_t(dx,dm')}
        {\int_{\mathbb{S}} o(\tilde{s},y_{t+1})
        \int_{\mathbb{X}}\mathcal{T}(d\tilde{x}\mid x,u_t)\,b_t(dx,d\tilde{m})}.
        \label{eq:bayesian_update}
    \end{equation}
    where we have used the factorization in \eqref{eq:augmented_transition} to
    integrate out the map component.
    The belief update \eqref{eq:belief_update}
    computes the posterior over the joint state space without
    assuming any factorization structure, in contrast to
    Rao-Blackwellized approaches~\cite{stachniss2009robotic} that maintain
    separate trajectory and map posteriors.
    % The predictive observation distribution is
    % \begin{align*}
    %     \label{eq:predictive_observation}
    %     \mathbf{G}(\,\cdot \mid b, u) \coloneq \mathbb{P}(y_{t+1}\in \cdot\mid b_{t}=b
    %     ,u_{t}=u)
    %     % \\&= \int_{\mathbb{X}} \int_{\mathbb{X}\times \mathbb{M}}
    %     % \mathcal{O}(\,\cdot\mid x_{t+1},m_{t}) \mathcal{T}(dx_{t+1}\mid x_{t},u_{t})
    %     % b_{t}(dx_{t},dm_{t}).
    % \end{align*}
    The POMDP reduces to a fully observable Markov decision process (MDP), often referred to as belief-MDP. It is fully defined by the 4-tuple
    $(\mathbb{B}, \mathbb{U}, \eta , \rho)$ with belief transition kernel
    \begin{equation}
        \eta(\,\cdot  \mid b, u) = \int_{\mathbb{Y}} \delta_{\mathbf{F}(b,
        u, y)}(\,\cdot \,)
        \, \mathbf{G}(dy \mid b, u),
        \label{eq:filter_kernel}
    \end{equation}
    where $\mathbf{G}(\,\cdot \mid b, u) \coloneq 
    \mathbb{P}(y_{t+1}\in \cdot\mid b_{t}=b, u_{t}=u)$
    is the predictive observation distribution,
    and one-stage cost
    \begin{equation}
        \rho(b_t, u_t) = r(b_{t},u_{t}) + \int_{\mathbb{S}} c(s_t, u_t) \, b_t(ds_t),
        \label{eq:expected_cost}
    \end{equation}
    where $c:\mathbb{S}\times \mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a state-dependent
    cost and $r:\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})\times \mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a
    belief-dependent cost encouraging exploration.

    The information the decision maker has access to include past measurements
    and control actions; we denote the collection of information available at
    time $t\ge 0$ as $I_{t}=\{y_{[0,t]},u_{[0,t-1]}\}$ with $I_{0}=\{y_{0}\}$,
    where we use the notation $y_{[0,t]}=\{y_{k}\in\mathbb{Y},0\le~k\le~t\}$,
    $u_{[0,t-1]}=\{u_{k}\in\mathbb{U},0\le~k\le~t-1\}.$
    We denote the control policy as $\gamma=\{\gamma_{t}\}_{t\ge0}$.
    At time $t$, we have that $\gamma_{t}:\mathbb{Y}^{t}\times\mathbb{U}^{t-1}\to\mathbb{U}$ 
    or $u_{t}=\gamma_{t}(I_{t})$.
    We let $\Gamma$ denote the set of admissible control policies and $\Gamma^{s}$
    denote the set of stationary policies.
    The goal is to minimize the infinite horizon discounted cost:
    \begin{equation}
        \tilde{J}(b_{0},\gamma)\coloneq \lim_{T \to \infty}
        \mathbb{E}_{b_{0}}^{\gamma}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \beta^{t}
        \rho(b_{t},u_{t}) \right],
        \label{eq:infinite_horizon}
    \end{equation}
    where $\mathbb{E}_{b_{0}}^{\gamma}$ is the expectation with initial
    distribution $s_{0}\sim b_{0}$ under policy $\gamma$.

\section{Properties of Active SLAM}\label{sec:Properties of Active SLAM} % (fold)
    The belief MDP formulation established in Section~\ref{sub:belief_mdp}
    provides a rigorous mathematical framework for active SLAM, but its
    practical utility depends on verifying key structural properties of the
    belief dynamics. This section establishes two fundamental results: first,
    that the belief process $\{b_t, u_t\}_{t \geq 0}$ forms a controlled
    Markov chain (Theorem~\ref{thm:cmc}), confirming that the belief is indeed
    a sufficient statistic for optimal control \cite{yushkevich1976reduction}; and second, that the belief
    transition kernel $\eta$ satisfies a weak continuity property called the
    weak Feller condition (Theorem~\ref{thm:weakfeller}), which ensures small
    changes in beliefs and actions produce small changes in posterior
    distributions.

    Verifying the weak Feller property directly from the definition
    requires establishing probabilistic continuity properties of the transition
    kernel $\mathcal{T}$ and observation kernel $\mathcal{O}$, which may be unfamiliar
    to practitioners coming from robotics backgrounds. 
    % We therefore provide two sets of sufficient conditions
    % (Assumptions~\ref{ass:3}--\ref{ass:4})
    We therefore provide sufficient conditions (Assumption \ref{ass:3})
    expressed in terms of standard continuity of the motion and measurement
    models $f$ and $g$. These conditions are
    straightforward to verify for common robotic systems and imply the
    requisite probabilistic continuity properties.
    We begin by formalizing the Markov structure of the belief process.
    \begin{theorem}[{\cite[Theorem~1]{gusija2026slam}}]
        The belief process $\{ b_{t}, u_{t} \} _{t\ge 0}$ is a controlled
        Markov chain.
        \label{thm:cmc}
    \end{theorem}

    Furthermore, the belief $b_t$ is a sufficient statistic for optimal control \cite{yushkevich1976reduction}, and the stage cost \eqref{eq:expected_cost} is a function of the belief.

    To state the weak Feller property precisely, we first recall the notion of
    weak convergence of probability measures. A sequence of probability
    measures $\{\mu_n\}_{n \geq 1}$ on a metric space $\mathbb{X}$ converges
    weakly to $\mu$, written as $\mu_{n}\to \mu$ weakly, if
    \begin{equation*}
        \int_{\mathbb{X}} h(x) \, \mu_n(dx) \xrightarrow[n \to \infty]{} \int_{\mathbb{X}} h(x) \, \mu(dx)
    \end{equation*}
    for every bounded continuous function $h: \mathbb{X} \to
    \mathbb{R}$.
    The belief transition kernel $\eta$ has the \emph{weak Feller property} if
    $(b_n, u_n) \to (b, u)$ implies $\eta(\,\cdot \mid b_n, u_n) \to
    \eta(\,\cdot \mid b, u)$ weakly.
    We present the following set of assumptions.
    \begin{assumption}[\cite{feinberg2016partially}]
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item []
            \item The transition probability $\mathcal{T}(\,\cdot \mid x,u)$ is 
                weak Feller.
            \item The observation kernel $\mathcal{O}(\,\cdot \mid x,m,u)$ is continuous
                in total variation.
        \end{enumerate}
        \label{ass:1}
    \end{assumption}
    The following assumptions provide sufficient conditions that are
    straightforward to check for typical robotic systems.
    \begin{assumption}[Sufficient conditions for Assumption \ref{ass:1}]
         A robot is equipped with a motion model $x_{t+1}=f(x_{t},u_{t},\xi_{t})$
         as described in \eqref{eq:robot_dynamics}, that is continuous in
         $(x_{t},u_{t})$ and a measurement model $y_{t}=g(x_{t}, m_{t},
         u_{t})+\zeta_{t}$ that is continuous in $(x_{t}, m_{t}, u_{t})$ and $\zeta_t$ admits a continuous density with respect to some reference measure.
    \label{ass:3}
    \end{assumption}
    \begin{remark}[Verification for common models]
        Assumption~\ref{ass:3} permits multiplicative or state-dependent noise, requiring only that $f(x,u,\xi)$ be continuous in $(x,u)$ for each fixed $\xi$.
    The unicycle and Dubins airplane models satisfy 
    this: for fixed $\xi$, the maps $(x,u) \mapsto f(x,u,\xi)$ are continuous. 
    When paired with a sensor whose observation 
    dynamics $g(x,m,u) + \zeta$ are continuous in $(x,m,u)$ with continuous density for $\zeta$, such as a range-bearing sensor with additive Gaussian noise, Assumption~\ref{ass:3} holds.
    \end{remark}
    
    We now have the following result,
    \begin{theorem}[{\cite[Theorem~2]{gusija2026slam}}]
        Provided that any one of Assumptions~\ref{ass:1} or~\ref{ass:3} hold,
        the belief transition kernel, $\eta$, of \eqref{eq:filter_kernel} is
        weak Feller. \label{thm:weakfeller}
    \end{theorem}

    Throughout the rest of this work, we assume the following. 
    \begin{assumption}
    The belief-MDP satisfies the following:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item The one-stage cost function $\rho:\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})\times\mathbb{U}\to\mathbb{R}$ \eqref{eq:expected_cost} is bounded and continuous.
            \item The belief transition $\eta$ is weak Feller.
            \item $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})$ and $\mathbb{U}$ are compact.
        \end{enumerate}
        \label{ass:6}
    \end{assumption}
    
    Up until this point we have spent our time validating the weak Feller
    property and the above assumptions; these now yield the following optimal
    policy existence result.
    \begin{theorem}\label{thm:existence}
        Under Assumption~\ref{ass:6}, there exists an optimal
        policy.
    \end{theorem}
    Theorem~\ref{thm:existence} guarantees that an optimal policy exists but does not suggest how to compute one; the belief space $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})$ is infinite-dimensional and the action space is uncountable. The next section develops a finite approximation that makes the problem tractable while preserving near-optimality guarantees.
% section Properties of Active SLAM (end)

\section{An Alternative Finite Window Approach}\label{sec:An Alternative Finite Window Approach} % (fold)
    This section adapts the finite-memory framework of
    \citet{kara2023convergence} to the SLAM belief MDP. The constructions of
    the information state, the approximate model, and the value and policy
    bounds follow their development, with the modifications required by the
    belief-dependent cost term $r$.

    Assume that our initial joint hidden state $S_{0}$ has a prior distribution
    $\kappa \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})$. Then, for the conditional distribution
    of $S_{t}$ given the history of information $h_{t}=\{
    y_{[0,t]},u_{[0,t-1]} \} $ (i.e., all the observations and 
    actions taken up until time $t$), we define
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbb{P}^{\kappa}(S_{t}\in \cdot \mid h_{t})\coloneq 
        \mathrm{Pr}(S_{t}\in \cdot \mid h_{t})
    .\end{equation*}
    Given that $s_{0}\sim \kappa $, we also define the following predictive observation
    distribution
    \begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{P}^{\kappa }(Y_{t}\in \cdot \mid h_{t}^{-})\coloneq 
    \mathrm{Pr}(Y_{t}\in \cdot \mid h_{t}^{-})
    .\end{equation*}
    for which $h_{t}=h_{t}^{-}\cup \{ y_{t} \}$ (i.e., $h_{t}^{-}$ excludes $y_{t}$).

    We now consider what is referred as the \emph{information state}
    \cite{kara2023convergence}
    \begin{equation}
        I_{t}=(b_{t-N}^{-},h_{t}^{N})
        \label{eq:information state}
    \end{equation}
    which for a memory size of $N\ge1$ is composed of the prior predictor
    \begin{equation*}
        b_{t-N}^{-}\coloneq \mathrm{Pr}(S_{t-N}\in \cdot \mid h_{t-N}^{-})
    \end{equation*}
    and the history of information within the prescribed window of memory
    \begin{equation}
        h_{t}^{N}= \begin{cases}
        \{ y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N-1,t-1]} \} & N>0\\
        y_{t} & N=0
        .\end{cases}
        \label{eq:history_var}
    \end{equation}
    The state space of this information state is defined as $\mathbb{I}\coloneq
    \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})\times \mathcal{D}^{N}$, where we equip $\mathbb{I}$
    with the product topology in which we consider the weak convergence
    topology on $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})$  and the usual topologies on
    $\mathcal{D}^{N}\coloneq \mathbb{Y}^{N+1}\times \mathbb{U}^{N}$, where
    $\mathcal{D}^{N}$ is referred to as the space of data.

    The information state can be mapped to the belief state $b_{t}$
    \eqref{eq:belief}. Consider the map $\Psi:\mathbb{I}\to \mathbb{B}$, for some
    $I_{t}=(b_{t-N}^{-},h_{t}^{N})$:
    \begin{align*}
        \Psi(I_{t})=\Psi(b_{t-N}^{-},h_{t}^{N})
        &= \mathbb{P}^{b_{t\!-\!N}^{-}}(S_{t}\in \cdot \mid h_{t}^{N})\\
        &= \mathbb{P}^{b_{t\!-\!N}^{-}}(S_{t}\in \cdot \mid y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N],t-1})\\
        &=\mathbb{P}^{\kappa }(S_{t}\in \cdot \mid y_{[0,t]},u_{[0,t-1]})\\
        &=\mathbb{P}^{\kappa }(S_{t}\in \cdot \mid h_{t})\\
        &=b_{t}
    \end{align*}
    such that the map $\Psi$ acts as the Bayesian update of $b_{t-N}^{-}$ using
    $h_{t}^{N}$. Using this map, we can define the stage-wise cost function and
    transition probabilities. We first consider the new cost function $\hat{\rho
    }:\mathbb{I}\times \mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{R} $ using the belief-dependent cost
    of the POMDP
    \begin{align}
        \label{eq:information stage cost}
        \hat{\rho }(I_{t},u_{t})
        &=\hat{\rho }(b_{t-N}^{-},h_{t}^{N},u_{t})
        =\rho(\Psi(b_{t-N}^{-},h_{t}^{N}),u_{t})\\
        &=r(\Psi(b_{t-N}^{-},h_{t}^{N}),u_{t})+\int\limits_{\mathbb{S}}
        c(s_{t},u_{t})\mathbb{P}^{b_{t-N}^{-}}(ds_{t}\mid h_{t}^{N})\nonumber
    .\end{align}
    Similarly to the gathered history of data, we denote $\mathbf{y}\in
    \mathbb{Y}^{N+1}$ such that $\mathbf{y}= \{
    \mathbf{y}_{1},...,\mathbf{y}_{N+1} \}$ and similarly for $\mathbf{u}\in
    \mathbb{U}^{N}$. Furthermore, for some $A\in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{I})$ such
    that $A=B\times \{ \mathbf{y},\mathbf{u} \}  $ where $B\in
    \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{B})$, we write
    \begin{align*}
        &\mathbb{P}(I_{t+1}\in A\mid I_{[0,t]},u_{[0,t]})
        =\mathbb{P}(b_{t-N+1}^{-}\in B,h_{t}^{N}=(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{u})
        \mid b_{[0,t-N]}^{-},h_{t})\\
        &=\mathbbm{1}_{\{(y_{[t-N+1,t]},u_{[t-N+1,t]})=(\mathbf{y}_{[1,N]},\mathbf{u})\}}
        \times \mathbbm{1}_{\{\phi(b_{t-N}^{-},y_{t-N},u_{t-N})\in B\}}
        \mathbb{P}^{b_{t-N}^{-}}(y_{t+1}=\mathbf{y}_{N+1}\mid y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t]})\\
        &=\mathbb{P}(b_{t-N+1}^{-}\in B,h_{t}^{N}=(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{u})\mid 
        b_{t-N}^{-},y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t]})\\
        &=\mathbb{P}(I_{t+1}\in A\mid I_{t},u_{t})\\
        &=:\int\limits_{A} \overline{\eta }(dI_{t+1}\mid I_{t},u_{t}),
    \end{align*}
    where the map $\phi$ generates the next predictor
    \begin{align*}
        b_{t-N+1}^{-}=\phi (b_{t-N}^{-},y_{t-N},u_{t-N})
        &=\phi (\mathbb{P}^{\kappa}(S_{t-N}\in \cdot \mid
        y_{[0,t-N-1]},u_{[0,t-N-1]}),y_{t-N},u_{t-N})\\
        &=\mathbb{P}^{\kappa}(S_{t-N+1}\in \cdot \mid y_{[0,t-N]},u_{[0,t-N]})
    .\end{align*}
    So, $\overline{\eta}$ defines a controlled transition model for the new states
    $I_{t+1}\in \mathbb{I}$. Then, we can define the fully observable
    information state MDP which we will refer to as the
    information MDP fully described by the 4-tuple
    \begin{equation*}
        (\mathbb{I},\mathbb{U},\overline{\eta },\hat{\rho }).
    \end{equation*}

    Any policy $\gamma :\mathbb{B}\to \mathbb{U}$ defined for the belief MDP can be
    extended to the newly defined information MDP using the map $\Psi$ and 
    defining $\overline{\gamma}\coloneq \gamma \circ \Psi$ such that
    \begin{equation*}
    \overline{\gamma }(I)=\gamma (\Psi (b))
    .\end{equation*}
    Hence, if an optimal policy can be found for the belief MDP, $\gamma ^{*}$, the
    policy $\overline{\gamma }^{*}=\gamma ^{*}\circ\Psi $ is an optimal policy for the 
    newly defined MDP.

    We now write the discounted cost optimality equation for the information MDP, 
    for which we define assuming the decision maker has observed at least $N$ 
    information variables:
    \begin{equation*}
    J^{*}_{\beta }(I)=\min_{u\in \mathbb{U}}\left( \hat{\rho }(I,u)+
    \beta \int\limits J^{*}_{\beta}(I')\overline{\eta}(d I'\mid I, u) \right)
    .\end{equation*}

    \subsection{Approximation of the Information MDP}\label{sub:Approximation of the Information MDP} % (fold)
    Finding an optimal policy over $\mathbb{I}\coloneq \mathbb{B}\times
    \mathcal{D}^{N}$ using conventional learning algorithms is prohibitive due
    to the infinite-dimensional nature of $\mathbb{B}$. 
    We are thus interested in applying an approximation to $\mathbb{I}$ that 
    leverages results from the filter stability literature that yield near
    optimal policies.

    The crux of this approach is to consider some arbitrary fixed prior $b^{*}\in
    \mathbb{B}$ where we can define our approximate information space as
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{I}^{N}_{b^{*}}=\{ (b^{*},y_{[0,N]},u_{[0,N-1]}):y_{[0,N]}\in \mathbb{Y}^{N+1},
        u_{[0,N-1]}\in \mathbb{U}^{N}\} 
        \label{eq:approx finite window set}
    \end{equation}
    such that the state at time $t$ is 
    \begin{equation}
        \hat{I}_{t}=(b^{*},h_{t}^{N})
        \label{eq:information_state}
    \end{equation}
    since $b^{*}$ is a constant, it is no longer a state variable, so the 
    effective state is simply $h_{t}^{N}\in \mathcal{D}^{N}$ where the space of 
    data is finite when $\mathbb{U},\mathbb{Y}$ are finite.
    The approximate stage cost remains the same as in \eqref{eq:information
    stage cost}. The controlled transition model is now defined as
    \begin{equation}
        \hat{\eta }(\hat{I}_{t+1}\mid \hat{I}_{t},u_{t})
        =\hat{\eta}(b^{*},h_{t+1}^{N}\mid b^{*},h_{t}^{N},u_{t})
        =\overline{\eta}(\mathbb{B},h_{t+1}^{N}\mid b^{*},h_{t}^{N},u_{t})
        \label{eq:approx transition}
    \end{equation}
    and the cost is defined as 
    \begin{equation}
        \hat{\rho}(\hat{I}_{t},u_{t})=\rho(\Psi(b^{*},h_{t}^{N}),u_{t}).
        \label{eq:aproxx cost}
    \end{equation}
    Filter stability results from the literature
    \cite{kara2023convergence} show that under certain
    conditions the history of data washes out the incorrect prior in the ensuing
    filter updates and so, provided a large enough window of memory, policies
    fashioned using the fixed prior are near optimal when used on the original
    MDP. Prior analyses rely on the state transition being contractive 
    whereas the SLAM state includes a static map element. As a result, the SLAM
    setup will require additional analysis to verify that we can utilize
    results from filter stability to ensure the near optimality of approximate
    policies.

    % subsection Approximation of the Information MDP (end)
    \subsection{Approximation Error of the Value Function}\label{sec:Approximation Error of the Value Function} % (fold)
    Let us define the \emph{filter stability error} \cite{kara2023convergence} as
    \begin{equation}
        L_{t}^{N}:=\sup_{\hat{\gamma}\in\hat{\Gamma}}\mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}^{\hat{\gamma}}\left[
            \left\lVert \mathbb{P}^{b_{t}^{-}}(S_{t+N}\in\cdot\mid
            Y_{[t,t+N]},U_{[t,t+N-1]})-\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_{t+N}\in\cdot\mid
            Y_{[t,t+N]},U_{[t,t+N-1]}) \right\rVert _{TV}  \right]
        \label{eq:filter_stability_error}
    \end{equation}
    which measures the robustness of the filter when initialized with the
    arbitrary fixed prior $b^{*}$ of \eqref{eq:information_state} in place of
    the proper prior $b_{0}^{-}$.

    Following procedure set out in \citet{kara2023convergence}, the goal is to
    bound the approximation error of the value function in terms of this filter
    stability error and show that under conditions appropriate to the SLAM
    model, the error vanishes as $N\to \infty $. We begin by deriving the
    approximation error of the value function for which we introduce the
    following notation:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $J^{*}_{\beta}$ is the optimal value function for the base MDP.
        \item $J^{N}_{\beta}$ is the optimal value function for the approximate
            MDP on the approximate information state space
            $\mathbb{I}_{b^{*}}^{N}$.
        \item $\tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}$ is the optimal value function for the
            approximate MDP on the  information state space $\mathbb{I}$.
    \end{itemize}

    Before we proceed we must make an additional assumption on the
    belief-dependent term of the cost function.
    \begin{assumption}
        The belief-dependent cost $r:\mathbb{B}\times \mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{R}$ is Lipschitz in total variation, i.e., for some $D>0$ and $b,b'\in \mathbb{B}$,
        \begin{equation*}
            | r(b)-r(b') |\le D\lVert b-b' \rVert_{TV}.
        \end{equation*}
        \label{ass:lipschitz_cost}
    \end{assumption}

    First, it makes sense that we should show that this holds for
    our stage cost $\tilde{W}_{1}$.
    \begin{proposition}
        For $b,b'\in\mathbb{B}$,
        \begin{equation*}
            \bigl|\tilde{W}_{1}(b)-\tilde{W}_{1}(b')\bigr|
            \le\lVert d_{\mathbb{S}}\rVert_{\infty}\,
            \lVert b-b'\rVert_{TV}.
        \end{equation*}
        \label{prop:rao_lipschitz}
    \end{proposition}
    \begin{proof}
        Let $\sigma\coloneq b-b'$. We note the following difference of squares-like
        identity 
        \begin{equation*}
            b\otimes b-b'\otimes b'=\sigma\otimes b+b'\otimes\sigma
        \end{equation*}
        which gives
        \begin{equation*}
            \bigl|\tilde{W}_{1}(b)-\tilde{W}_{1}(b')\bigr|
            \le\Bigl|\int_{\mathbb{S}}\psi_{b}(s')\,\sigma(ds')\Bigr|
            +\Bigl|\int_{\mathbb{S}}\psi_{b'}(s)\,\sigma(ds)\Bigr|,
            \qquad
            \psi_{b}(s')\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{S}}d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s')\,b(ds).
        \end{equation*}
        Since $b,b'$ are probability measures, 
        \begin{equation*}
            \sigma(\mathbb{S})=(b-b')(\mathbb{S})=b(\mathbb{S})-b'(\mathbb{S})=1-1=0,
        \end{equation*} 
        and hence 
        \begin{equation}
            \int c\,d\sigma=0,\, \forall c\in\mathbb{R}
            \label{eq:constant_annihilation}
        \end{equation}
        
        Setting $c_{b}\coloneq\tfrac12\bigl(\inf_{s'}\psi_{b}(s')
        +\sup_{s'}\psi_{b}(s')\bigr)$,
        \begin{align*}
            \Bigl|\int_{\mathbb{S}}\psi_{b}\,d\sigma\Bigr|
            &=\Bigl|\int_{\mathbb{S}}(\psi_{b}-c_{b})\,d\sigma\Bigr|\\
            &\le\lVert\psi_{b}-c_{b}\rVert_{\infty}\,\lVert\sigma\rVert_{TV}\\
            &=\tfrac12\bigl(\sup\psi_{b}-\inf\psi_{b}\bigr)
            \lVert\sigma\rVert_{TV}\\
            &\le\tfrac12\lVert d_{\mathbb{S}}\rVert_{\infty}
            \lVert\sigma\rVert_{TV},
        \end{align*}
        where the first equality uses \eqref{eq:constant_annihilation},
        the inequality is the duality bound
        $\bigl|\int f\,d\sigma\bigr|\le\lVert f\rVert_{\infty}
        \lVert\sigma\rVert_{TV}$ applied to $f=\psi_{b}-c_{b}$,
        the third step is the identity
        $\lVert\psi_{b}-c_{b}\rVert_{\infty}
        =\tfrac12(\sup\psi_{b}-\inf\psi_{b})$ for $c_b$ the midpoint of
        the range of $\psi_{b}$, and the last step uses
        $0\le\psi_{b}\le\lVert d_{\mathbb{S}}\rVert_{\infty}$, valid since
        $\psi_{b}$ is an average of $d_{\mathbb{S}}$ on the compact space
        $\mathbb{S}$. The identical
        argument applies to $\psi_{b'}$. Summing the two bounds concludes the
        proof.
    \end{proof}
    \begin{theorem}[{\cite[Theorem~2]{kara2023convergence}}]
        Under Assumption~\ref{ass:lipschitz_cost}, for
        $I_{0}=(b_{0}^{-},h_{0}^{N})$, with a policy $\hat{\gamma}$ acting on
        the first $N$ steps of the process that produces $h_{0}^{N}$, we then
        have
        \begin{equation}
            \mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}^{\hat{\gamma}}\left[ \left|
            \tilde{J}_{\beta}^{N}(I_{0})-J_{\beta}^{*}(I_{0}) \right| \mid
            h^{N}_{0} \right] \le \left(D+\frac{\lVert c \rVert
                _{\infty}+\lVert r \rVert
            _{\infty}}{1-\beta}\right)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t}L_{t}^{N}.
            \label{eq:approx_bound_1}
        \end{equation}
        where $\tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(I_{0})$ is the optimal value function for the approximate MDP.
        \label{thm:approx_bound}
    \end{theorem}

    Before we prove this theorem we must make use of the following lemma.
    \begin{lemma}[{\cite[Lemma~B.1]{kara2023convergence}}]
        For any $b,b^{*}\in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})$ and for any $(y,u)_{[t-N,t]}\in (\mathbb{Y}\times \mathbb{U})^{N}$,
        \begin{align*}
        &\lVert \mathbb{P}^{b}(Y_{t+1}\in\cdot\mid(y,u)_{[t-N,t]})-\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(Y_{t+1}\in\cdot\mid(y,u)_{[t-N,t]}) \rVert_{TV} \\
        &\le \lVert \mathbb{P}^{b}(S_{t}\in\cdot\mid y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t-1]})-\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_{t}\in\cdot\mid y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t-1]}) \rVert _{TV}.
        \end{align*}
        \label{lem:observation_contraction}
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
        Let $f\in M(\mathbb{Y})$ (i.e., a measurable function of $\mathbb{Y}$) such that $\lVert f \rVert_{\infty}\le1$. We write
        \begin{align*}
        &\int f(y_{t+1}) \, \mathbb{P}^{b}(dy_{t+1}\mid(y,u)_{[t-N,t]})- \int f(y_{t+1}) \, \mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(dy_{t+1}\mid(y,u)_{[t-N,t]})\\
        &= \int f(y_{t+1})\mathcal{O}(y_{t+1}\mid s_{t+1})\mathcal{S}(ds_{t+1}\mid s_{t},u_{t}) \, \mathbb{P}^{b}(ds_{t}\mid y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t-1]}) \\
        &-  \int f(y_{t+1})\mathcal{O}(y_{t+1}\mid s_{t+1})\mathcal{S}(ds_{t+1}\mid s_{t},u_{t}) \, \mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(ds_{t}\mid y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t-1]})\\
        &\le \lVert \mathbb{P}^{b}(S_{t}\in\cdot\mid y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t-1]})-\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_{t}\in\cdot\mid y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t-1]}) \rVert_{TV}
        \end{align*}
        with the last step using the fact that $\int f(y_{t+1})\mathcal{O}(dy_{t+1}\mid s_{t+1})\mathcal{S}(ds_{t+1}\mid s_{t},u_{t})$ is bounded by one as a function of $x_{t}$ for $\lVert f \rVert_{\infty}\le 1$. Taking the supremum over all $\lVert f \rVert_{\infty}\le 1$ concludes the proof.
    \end{proof}

    We now proceed to the proof.

    \begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{thm:approx_bound}]
    Let $I_{0}=(b^{-}_{0},h^{N}_{1})$. Then, we write the optimal value function for the approximate MDP as
    \begin{equation*}
    \tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(I_{0})=J_{\beta}^{N}(b^{*},h_{1}^{N})=\min_{u_{1}\in \mathbb{U}}\left( \hat{\rho}(b^{*},y_{1},y_{0},u_{0},u_{1})+\beta \sum_{y_{2}\in \mathbb{Y}}J^{N}_{\beta}(b^{*},y_{2},y_{1},u_{1}) \mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(y_{2}\mid y_{1},y_{0},u_{1},u_{0})\right).
    \end{equation*}
    Furthermore,
    \begin{align*}
    &J^{*}_{\beta}(I_{0})=J^{*}_{\beta}(b_{0}^{-},y_{1},y_{0},u_{0})\\
    &= \min_{u_{1}\in \mathbb{U}}\left( \hat{\rho}(b^{-}_{0},y_{1},y_{0},u_{0},u_{1})+\beta \sum_{y_{2}\in \mathbb{Y}}J^{*}_{\beta}(b^{-}_{0},y_{2},y_{1},u_{1}) \mathbb{P}^{b^{-}_{0}}(y_{2}\mid y_{1},y_{0},u_{1},u_{0})\right).
    \end{align*}
    Note that for the approximate value function, any choice of belief in place of $b^{*}$ yields an identical cost provided the other terms are the same, i.e., for any $b\in\mathbb{B}$
    \begin{equation*}
        \tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(b,y_{2},y_{1},u_{1})=\tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(b^{*},y_{2},y_{1},u_{1})=J_{\beta}^{N}(b^{*},y_{2},y_{1},y_{0}).
    \end{equation*}
    Specifically, we would like to make use of the following fact that results from the above
    \begin{equation*}
        J^{N}_{\beta}(b^{*},y_{2},y_{1},u_{1})=\tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(b_{1}^{-}(b_{0}^{-},y_{0},u_{0}),y_{2},y_{1},u_{1}).
    \end{equation*}
    Hence, we can write the following:
    \begin{align*}
    &| \tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(I_{0})-J^{*}_{\beta}(I_{0}) |\le \max_{u_{1}\in \mathbb{U}} \left| \hat{\rho}(b^{*},y_{1},y_{0},u_{0},u_{1})- \hat{\rho}(b_{0}^{-},y_{1},y_{0},u_{0},u_{1}) \right| \\
    &+\max_{u_{1}\in \mathbb{U}}\beta \left| \sum_{y_{2}\in \mathbb{Y}}J^{N}_{\beta}(b^{*},y_{2},y_{1},u_{1}) \left[\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(y_{2}\mid y_{1},y_{0},u_{1},u_{0})- \mathbb{P}^{b^{-}_{0}}(y_{2}\mid y_{1},y_{0},u_{1},u_{0})\right]  \right| \\
    &+\max_{u_{1}\in \mathbb{U}}\beta \sum_{y_{2}\in \mathbb{Y}}\left| \tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(b_{1}^{-}(b_{0},y_{0},u_{0}),y_{2},y_{1},u_{1})-J_{\beta}^{*}(b_{1}^{-}(b_{0}^{-},y_{0},u_{0}),y_{2},y_{1},u_{1}) \right| \mathbb{P}^{b_{0}^{-}}(y_{2}\mid y_{1},y_{0},u_{1},u_{0}).
    \end{align*}
    Note, by definition of $\hat{\rho}$, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \left| \hat{\rho}(b^{*},y_{1},y_{0},u_{0},u_{1})- \hat{\rho}(b_{0}^{-},y_{1},y_{0},u_{0},u_{1}) \right|
    &\le\left|r(\Psi(b^{*},y_{1},y_{0},u_{0}),u_{1})-r(\Psi(b_{0}^{-},y_{1},y_{0},u_{0}),u_{1})\right|\\
    &\!\!\!\!\!+\lVert c \rVert _{\infty}\cdot\lVert \mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_{1}\in\cdot\mid y_{1},y_{0},u_{0})-\mathbb{P}^{b_{0}^{-}}(S_{1}\in\cdot\mid y_{1},y_{0},u_{0}) \rVert_{TV} \\
    &\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\le (D+\lVert c \rVert _{\infty})\lVert \mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_{1}\in\cdot\mid y_{1},y_{0},u_{0})-\mathbb{P}^{b_{0}^{-}}(S_{1}\in\cdot\mid y_{1},y_{0},u_{0}) \rVert_{TV}.
    \end{align*}
    If we denote $I_{1}=(b_{1}^{-}(b_{0},y_{0},u_{0}),y_{2},y_{1},u_{1})$, using \cref{lem:observation_contraction}, we can write
    \begin{align*}
    &\mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}^{\gamma}\left[ \left| \tilde{J}_{\beta}^{N}(I_{0})-J_{\beta}^{*}(I_{0}) \right|  \right] \le (D+\lVert c \rVert _{\infty})\mathbb{E}_{b^{-}_{0}}^{\gamma}\left[ \lVert \mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_{1}\in\cdot\mid Y_{1},Y_{0},U_{0})-\mathbb{P}^{b_{0}^{-}}(S_{1}\in\cdot\mid Y_{1},Y_{0},U_{0}) \rVert_{TV}   \right] \\
    &+\max_{u_{1}\in \mathbb{U}}\beta \lVert J_{\beta}^{N} \rVert _{\infty}\mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}\left[ \lVert \mathbb{P}^{b_{0}^{-}}(y_{2}\mid Y_{1},Y_{0},U_{1},U_{0})-\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(y_{2}\mid Y_{1},Y_{0},U_{1},U_{0}) \rVert_{TV}  \right]  \\
    &+\max_{u_{1}\in \mathbb{U}}\beta \mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}^{\gamma}\left[ \sum_{y_{2}\in \mathbb{Y}}\left| \tilde{J}_{\beta}^{N}(I_{1})-J^{*}_{\beta}(I_{1}) \right|\mathbb{P}^{b_{0}^{-}}(y_{2}\mid Y_{1},Y_{0},u_{1},U_{0})  \right] \\
    &\le(D+\lVert c \rVert _{\infty}+\beta \lVert J_{\beta}^{N} \rVert _{\infty})L_{0}+\max_{u_{1}\in \mathbb{U}}\beta \mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}^{\gamma}\left[ \sum_{y_{2}\in \mathbb{Y}}\left| \tilde{J}_{\beta}^{N}(I_{1})-J^{*}_{\beta}(I_{1}) \right|\mathbb{P}^{b_{0}^{-}}(y_{2}\mid Y_{1},Y_{0},u_{1},U_{0})  \right]\\
    &\le(D+\lVert c \rVert _{\infty}+\beta \lVert J_{\beta}^{N} \rVert _{\infty})L_{0}+\sup_{\hat{\gamma}\in\hat{\Gamma}}\beta \mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}^{\hat{\gamma}}\left[\left| \tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(I_{1})-J_{\beta}^{*}(I_{1}) \right|  \right]
    \end{align*}
    where
    \begin{equation*}
        L_{t}^{N}:=\sup_{\hat{\gamma}\in\hat{\Gamma}}\mathbb{E}^{\hat{\gamma}}_{b_{0}^{-}}\left[ \lVert \mathbb{P}^{b_{t}^{-}}(S_{t+N}\in\cdot\mid Y_{[t,t+N]},U_{[t,t+N]})-\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_{t+N}\in\cdot\mid Y_{[t,t+N]},U_{[t,t+N]}) \rVert_{TV}  \right].
    \end{equation*}
    Then, following the same steps for $\mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}^{\hat{\gamma}}\left[\left| \tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(I_{1})-J_{\beta}^{*}(I_{1}) \right|  \right]$ and repeating the procedure, one can see that
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}\left[ \left|
        \tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(I_{0})-J_{\beta}^{*}(I_{0}) \right|  \right]
        \le(D+\lVert c \rVert _{\infty}+\beta \lVert J_{\beta}^{N} \rVert
        _{\infty})\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t}L_{t}^{N}.
    \end{equation*}
    Note that $\lVert J_{\beta}^{N} \rVert_{\infty}\le \frac{\lVert c \rVert_{\infty}+\lVert r \rVert_{\infty}}{1-\beta}$. 
    Hence, we can conclude
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}\left[ \left| \tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(I_{0})-J_{\beta}^{*}(I_{0}) \right|  \right] \le \left(D+\frac{\lVert c \rVert _{\infty}+\lVert r \rVert _{\infty}}{1-\beta}\right)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t}L_{t}^{N}.
    \end{equation*}
    \end{proof}

    \begin{theorem}[{\cite[Theorem~3]{kara2023convergence}}]
        Under Assumption~\ref{ass:lipschitz_cost}, for
        $I_{0}=(b_{0}^{-},h^{N}_{0})$, with a policy $\hat{\gamma}$ acting on the first $N$ steps,
        \begin{equation*}
            \mathbb{E}_{b_{0}^{-}}^{\hat{\gamma}}\left[ \left|
            \tilde{J}_{\beta}^{N}(I_{0})-J_{\beta}^{*}(I_{0}) \right| \mid
            h^{N}_{0} \right] \le 2\left(D+\frac{\lVert c \rVert
                _{\infty}+\lVert r \rVert
            _{\infty}}{1-\beta}\right)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t}L_{t}^{N}.
        \end{equation*}
        where $\gamma^{*,N}$ is the optimal policy of the approximate MDP applied to the original MDP.
        \label{thm:policy_bound}
    \end{theorem}
    We have now established an upper bound on the approximation error of the 
    value function. Unfortunately, the bound of
    Theorem~\ref{thm:approx_bound} cannot be salvaged in total variation
    for the SLAM model. Note that the bound is unhelpful unless the filter
    stability error \eqref{eq:filter_stability_error} vanishes as $N\to\infty$,
    which requires the posteriors initialized at $b_t^-$ and at $b^*$
    respectively to merge in total variation. For the SLAM state defined on
    $\mathbb{S}=\mathbb{X}\times\mathbb{M}$ this fails as the map component is
    static, the joint transition kernel
    $\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{T}\otimes\delta_m$ has Dobrushin coefficient zero,
    and every mixing-based total variation stability argument (e.g.,
    \cite{kara2023convergence,mcdonald2020exponential}) degenerates. Indeed,
    for a continuous map space, a map posterior admitting a density remains at
    maximal total variation distance from the Dirac measure at the true map for
    every finite window size $N$, however informative the data. The property
    that must drive the map marginal is instead posterior consistency, which is
    the concentration of the map posterior at the true map $m^{*}$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbb{P}^{b}(M_{t+N}\in\cdot\mid h_t^N)\to\delta_{m^*}\text{ weakly}
    \end{equation*}
    where the filter stability error is evaluated by having both posteriors
    converge to a common limit. Posterior consistency does not hold with
    respect to the total variation metric but does hold for any metric that
    metrizes the weak convergence topology such as the 1-Wasserstein metric (as
    we will explore in 
    Section~\ref{sec:Approximation Error via Wasserstein Regularity}). We note
    that for a finite map space the above results apply in total variation as
    stated. Nevertheless, on continuous map spaces any formulation of filter
    stability for the map marginal in total variation is not usable, and
    reformulating the filter stability error in terms of a weaker metric is
    required.
    % subsection Approximation Error of the Value Function (end)

    \subsection{Approximation Error via Wasserstein Regularity}
    \label{sec:Approximation Error via Wasserstein Regularity}
    We now present an approximation bound in which the filter stability
    error is measured with respect to the Wasserstein-$1$ metric. As stated 
    above, the desired property we would like to invoke is posterior consistency
    a property of Bayesian inference studied in literature concerning parameter
    estimation. %TODO% add citation
    In general, posterior consistency posits that a posterior distribution or belief
    over a static parameter will weakly converge to the degenerate distribution
    of that parameter under some conditions, so in the case of active mapping 
    (and after imposing some assumptions) posterior consistency says 
    \begin{equation*}
        b_{t}\to\delta_{m^{*}}\quad\text{weakly}
    \end{equation*}
    for the map posterior $b_t\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{M})$, where $m^*$ is the
    true map. On compact $\mathbb{M}$ the weak convergence topology
    is metrized by $W_1$, so consistency is equivalent to
    \begin{equation*}
        W_{1}(b_{t},\delta_{m^{*}})\to 0.
    \end{equation*}
    The work in this section follows \cite{demirci2024refined} and exploits the
    product structure $\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{T}\otimes\delta_m$ of the SLAM
    transition kernel. We replace Assumption~\ref{ass:lipschitz_cost} with the
    following.

    \begin{assumption}
        \label{ass:wasserstein_reg}
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[]
            \item The pose transition kernel is Lipschitz in total
                variation: there exists $\alpha_{\mathcal{T}}>0$ such
                that for all $x,x'\in\mathbb{X}$ and $u\in\mathbb{U}$,
                \begin{equation*}
                    \lVert \mathcal{T}(\,\cdot\mid x,u)
                    -\mathcal{T}(\,\cdot\mid x',u)\rVert_{TV}
                    \le \alpha_{\mathcal{T}}\,
                    d_{\mathbb{X}}(x,x').
                \end{equation*}
            \item The observation kernel is Lipschitz in total variation
                in the map: there exists
                $\alpha_{\mathcal{O}}>0$ such that for all
                $x\in\mathbb{X}$, $m,m'\in\mathbb{M}$, and
                $u\in\mathbb{U}$,
                \begin{equation*}
                    \lVert\mathcal{O}(\,\cdot\mid x,m,u)
                    -\mathcal{O}(\,\cdot\mid x,m',u)\rVert_{TV}
                    \le \alpha_{\mathcal{O}}\,
                    d_{\mathbb{M}}(m,m').
                \end{equation*}
            \item The state-dependent cost $c:\mathbb{S}\times
                \mathbb{U}\to\mathbb{R}$ is Lipschitz in the state:
                there exists $K_c>0$ such that for all
                $s,s'\in\mathbb{S}$ and $u\in\mathbb{U}$,
                \begin{equation*}
                    |c(s,u)-c(s',u)|\le K_c\,d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s').
                \end{equation*}
            \item The belief-dependent cost $r:\mathbb{B}\times \mathbb{U}\to 
                \mathbb{R} $ is Lipschitz in $W_{1}$ in the belief: $\exists K_{r}>0$
                such that for all $b,b'\in \mathbb{B}$ and $u\in \mathbb{U}$
                \begin{equation*}
                    |r(b,u)-r(b',u)|\le K_{r}W_{1}(b,b')
                \end{equation*}
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{assumption}
    Like with Proposition~\ref{prop:rao_lipschitz} we first would like to show
    our stage cost satisfies Assumption~\ref{ass:wasserstein_reg}-(4)
    \begin{proposition}
        \label{prop:rao_W1_lipschitz}
        For any $b,b'\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})$,
        \begin{equation*}
            \bigl|\tilde{W}_1(b)-\tilde{W}_1(b')\bigr|
            \le 2\,W_1(b,b').
        \end{equation*}
    \end{proposition}
    \begin{proof}
        Let $\sigma\coloneq b-b'$. As in the proof of
        Proposition~\ref{prop:rao_lipschitz}, the identity
        $b\otimes b-b'\otimes b'=\sigma\otimes b+b'\otimes\sigma$
        gives
        \begin{align*}
            \bigl|\tilde{W}_1(b)-\tilde{W}_1(b')\bigr|
            &=\left|\int_{\mathbb{S}\times\mathbb{S}}
            d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s')\,d(b\otimes b)
            -\int_{\mathbb{S}\times\mathbb{S}}
            d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s')\,d(b'\otimes b')\right|\\
            &=\left|\int_{\mathbb{S}\times\mathbb{S}}
            d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s')\,d(\sigma\otimes b)
            +\int_{\mathbb{S}\times\mathbb{S}}
            d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s')\,d(b'\otimes\sigma)\right|\\
            &\le\left|\int_{\mathbb{S}}
            \underbrace{\int_{\mathbb{S}}
            d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s')\,b(ds)}_{\eqqcolon\;\psi_b(s')}
            \,\sigma(ds')\right|
            +\left|\int_{\mathbb{S}}
            \underbrace{\int_{\mathbb{S}}
            d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s')\,b'(ds')}_{\eqqcolon\;
            \psi_{b'}(s)}\,\sigma(ds)\right|.
        \end{align*}
        Both $\psi_b$ and $\psi_{b'}$ are $1$-Lipschitz:
        for any $s_1',s_2'\in\mathbb{S}$,
        \begin{align*}
            |\psi_b(s_1')-\psi_b(s_2')|
            &=\left|\int_{\mathbb{S}}
            \bigl[d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s_1')
            -d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s_2')\bigr]\,b(ds)\right|\\
            &\le\int_{\mathbb{S}}
            \bigl|d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s_1')
            -d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s_2')\bigr|\,b(ds)\\
            &\le\int_{\mathbb{S}}
            d_{\mathbb{S}}(s_1',s_2')\,b(ds)\\
            &=d_{\mathbb{S}}(s_1',s_2'),
        \end{align*}
        where the third line is the reverse triangle
        inequality for $d_{\mathbb{S}}$. The identical
        argument applies to $\psi_{b'}$. Hence
        $\psi_b,\psi_{b'}\in\mathrm{Lip}(\mathbb{S},1)$,
        and so
        \begin{align*}
            \left|\int_{\mathbb{S}}\psi_b(s')\,
            \sigma(ds')\right|
            &\le W_1(b,b'),\\
            \left|\int_{\mathbb{S}}\psi_{b'}(s)\,
            \sigma(ds)\right|
            &\le W_1(b,b').
        \end{align*}
        Therefore
        $\bigl|\tilde{W}_1(b)-\tilde{W}_1(b')\bigr|
        \le 2\,W_1(b,b')$.
    \end{proof}

    We now verify \cite[Lemma~1]{demirci2024refined}, which is analogous to
    Lemma~\ref{lem:observation_contraction} with the difference being that it
    replaces the total variation bound on the predictive observation difference
    with a Wasserstein bound on the posterior. The proof exploits the product
    structure of the transition kernel
    $\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{T}\otimes\delta_m$, and is a nontrivial extension of
    \cite[Lemma~1]{demirci2024refined} due to
    Assumption~\ref{ass:wasserstein_reg}-(1) being imposed only on the
    pose's transition kernel (and not on the state transition kernel).
    \begin{lemma}[{\cite[Lemma~1]{demirci2024refined}}]
        \label{lem:observation_wasserstein}
        Under Assumption~\ref{ass:wasserstein_reg}-(1,2),
        for any $b,b^{*}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S})$ and any
        $(y,u)_{[t-N,t]}\in(\mathbb{Y}\times\mathbb{U})^N$,
        \begin{align*}
            &\lVert \mathbb{P}^{b}(Y_{t+1}\in\cdot\mid
            (y,u)_{[t-N,t]})
            -\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(Y_{t+1}\in\cdot\mid
            (y,u)_{[t-N,t]})\rVert_{TV}\\
            &\quad\le \alpha^{*}\,
            W_1\!\bigl(\mathbb{P}^{b}(S_t\in\cdot\mid
            y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t-1]}),\,
            \mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_t\in\cdot\mid
            y_{[t-N,t]},u_{[t-N,t-1]})\bigr),
        \end{align*}
        where $\alpha^{*}
        =\max(\alpha_{\mathcal{T}},\alpha_{\mathcal{O}})$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
        Let $f\in M(\mathbb{Y})$ with $\lVert f\rVert_\infty\le1$.
        Following the same expansion as in the proof of
        Lemma~\ref{lem:observation_contraction}, define the function
        \begin{align*}
            h(x_t,m_t)&\coloneq
            \int\limits_{\mathbb{X}\times \mathbb{M}}
            \biggl[\int_{\mathbb{Y}} f(y_{t+1})\,\mathcal{O}(dy_{t+1}\mid
            x_{t+1},m_{t+1},u_t) \biggr]
            \delta_{m_{t}}(dm_{t+1})\mathcal{T}(dx_{t+1}\mid x_t,u_t)\\
                      &=\int_{\mathbb{X}} \biggl[\int_{\mathbb{Y}}
            f(y_{t+1})\,\mathcal{O}(dy_{t+1}\mid x_{t+1},m_t,u_t) \biggr]
            \mathcal{T}(dx_{t+1}\mid x_t,u_t),
        \end{align*}
        where we have used $\mathcal{S}
        =\mathcal{T}\otimes\delta_{m}$. We then have
        \begin{align*}
            &\int f(y_{t+1})\,\mathbb{P}^{b}(Y_{t+1}\in dy_{t+1}\mid
            (y,u)_{[t-N,t]})
            -\int f(y_{t+1})\,\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(Y_{t+1}\in dy_{t+1}\mid
            (y,u)_{[t-N,t]})\\
            &=\int_{\mathbb{S}} h(s_t)\,[\mathbb{P}^{b}(S_{t}\in ds_{t}\mid h_t)
            -\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_{t}\in ds_{t}\mid h_t)].
        \end{align*}
        It remains to show $h$ is $\alpha^{*}$-Lipschitz in
        $s=(x,m)$ under $d_{\mathbb{S}}(s,s')
        =d_{\mathbb{X}}(x,x')+d_{\mathbb{M}}(m,m')$.

        Write $\omega(x_{t+1},m)
        =\int f(y)\,\mathcal{O}(dy\mid x_{t+1},m,u_t)$,
        so that $h(x,m)=\int\omega(x_{t+1},m)\,
        \mathcal{T}(dx_{t+1}\mid x,u_t)$ and
        $\lVert\omega\rVert_\infty\le 1$.

        \textit{Lipschitz in $x$:} For fixed $m$,
        \begin{align*}
            |h(x,m)-h(x',m)|
            &=\Bigl|\int\omega(x_{t+1},m)
            \bigl[\mathcal{T}(dx_{t+1}\mid x,u_t)
            -\mathcal{T}(dx_{t+1}\mid x',u_t)\bigr]\Bigr|\\
            &\le \lVert\mathcal{T}(\cdot\mid x,u_t)
            -\mathcal{T}(\cdot\mid x',u_t)\rVert_{TV}\\
            &\le\alpha_{\mathcal{T}}\,d_{\mathbb{X}}(x,x'),
        \end{align*}
        using $\lVert\omega\rVert_\infty\le 1$ and
        Assumption~\ref{ass:wasserstein_reg}-(1).

        \textit{Lipschitz in $m$:} For fixed $x$,
        \begin{align*}
            |h(x,m)-h(x,m')|
            &=\Bigl|\int\bigl[\omega(x_{t+1},m)
            -\omega(x_{t+1},m')\bigr]
            \mathcal{T}(dx_{t+1}\mid x,u_t)\Bigr|\\
            &\le\int\lVert\mathcal{O}(\cdot\mid x_{t+1},m,u_t)
            -\mathcal{O}(\cdot\mid x_{t+1},m',u_t)
            \rVert_{TV}\,
            \mathcal{T}(dx_{t+1}\mid x,u_t)\\
            &\le\alpha_{\mathcal{O}}\,
            d_{\mathbb{M}}(m,m'),
        \end{align*}
        using $\lVert f\rVert_\infty\le 1$ and
        Assumption~\ref{ass:wasserstein_reg}-(2). Combining via the triangle
        inequality,
        \begin{equation*}
            |h(x,m)-h(x',m')|
            \le\alpha_{\mathcal{T}}\,d_{\mathbb{X}}(x,x')
            +\alpha_{\mathcal{O}}\,d_{\mathbb{M}}(m,m')
            \le\alpha^{*}\,d_{\mathbb{S}}((x,m),(x',m')).
        \end{equation*}
        Therefore $h/\alpha^{*}\in\mathrm{Lip}(\mathbb{S},1)$ and so
        \begin{equation*}
            \Bigl|\int h(s_t)\,[\mathbb{P}^{b}(ds_{t}\in\cdot\mid h_t)
            -\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(ds_{t}\in\cdot\mid h_t)]\Bigr|
            \le\alpha^{*}\,W_1\bigl(
            \mathbb{P}^{b}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h_t),\,
            \mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h_t)\bigr).
        \end{equation*}
        Taking the supremum over $\lVert f\rVert_\infty\le 1$
        concludes the proof.
    \end{proof}

    Define the \emph{Wasserstein filter stability error}
    \begin{equation}
        \bar{L}_t^{N}\coloneq\sup_{\hat{\gamma}\in\hat{\Gamma}}
        \mathbb{E}^{\hat{\gamma}}_{b_0^{-}}\!\left[
        W_1\!\left(
        \mathbb{P}^{b_t^{-}}(S_{t+N}\in\cdot\mid
        Y_{[t,t+N]},U_{[t,t+N-1]}),\,
        \mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(S_{t+N}\in\cdot\mid
        Y_{[t,t+N]},U_{[t,t+N-1]})
        \right)\right]
        \label{eq:wasserstein_filter_stability}.
    \end{equation}
    We now state a result on the approximation error of the value function, 
    similar to Theorem~\ref{thm:approx_bound}, but this time in 
    terms of \eqref{eq:wasserstein_filter_stability}.
    \begin{theorem}[{\cite[Theorem~1]{demirci2024refined}}]
        \label{thm:wasserstein_approx_bound}
        Under Assumption
        \ref{ass:wasserstein_reg}, for
        $I_0=(b_0^{-},h_0^{N})$ with a policy $\hat{\gamma}$ acting
        on the first $N$ steps,
        \begin{equation}
            \mathbb{E}^{\hat{\gamma}}_{b_0^{-}}\!\left[
            \left|\tilde{J}^{N}_{\beta}(I_0)
            -J^{*}_{\beta}(I_0)\right|
            \,\bigg|\, h_0^{N}\right]
            \le\biggl(K_c+K_{r}
            +\frac{\alpha^{*}\beta
            (\lVert c\rVert_\infty
            +\lVert r\rVert_\infty)}{1-\beta}\biggr)
            \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^t\bar{L}_t^{N}.
            \label{eq:wasserstein_approx_bound}
        \end{equation}
    \end{theorem}
    \begin{proof}
        The proof follows the recursive structure of the proof of
        Theorem~\ref{thm:approx_bound}. We start with same upper bound of three
        terms:
        \begin{align*}
            \bigl|\tilde{J}^N_\beta(I_0)-J^*_\beta(I_0)\bigr|
            &\le\underbrace{\max_{u_1\in \mathbb{U}}\bigl|\hat{\rho}(b^*,h_{0},u_1)
            -\hat{\rho}(b_0^-,h_{0},u_1)\bigr|}_{\text{(I)}}\\
            &\quad+\underbrace{\max_{u_1\in \mathbb{U}}\beta\left|
            \sum_{y_2\in \mathbb{Y}}J^N_\beta(b^*,y_2,y_1,u_1)
            \bigl[\mathbb{P}^{b^*}(y_2\mid h_{0},u_1)
            -\mathbb{P}^{b_0^-}(y_2\mid h_{0},u_1)\bigr]
            \right|}_{\text{(II)}}\\
            &\quad+\underbrace{\max_{u_1\in \mathbb{U}}\beta
            \sum_{y_2\in \mathbb{Y}}
            \bigl|\tilde{J}^N_\beta(I_1)-J^*_\beta(I_1)\bigr|
            \,\mathbb{P}^{b_0^-}(y_2\mid h_{0},u_1)}_{\text{(III)}}.
        \end{align*}
        Term (III) provides the recursion and is handled identically.
        We bound terms (I) and (II) using $W_1$.

        By definition of $\hat{\rho}$
        \eqref{eq:information stage cost},
        \begin{align*}
            \bigl|\hat{\rho}(b^*,h_{0},u_1)
            -\hat{\rho}(b_0^-,h_{0},u_1)\bigr|
            &\le\bigl|r(\Psi(b^*,h_{0}),u_1)
            -r(\Psi(b_0^-,h_{0}),u_1)\bigr|\\
            &\quad+\Bigl|\int c(s_{1},u_1)
            \bigl[\mathbb{P}^{b^*}(S_{1}\in ds\mid h_{0})
            -\mathbb{P}^{b_0^-}(ds\mid h_{0})\bigr]\Bigr|.
        \end{align*} 
        For the state cost, $c(\cdot,u_1)$ is $K_c$-Lipschitz by
        Assumption~\ref{ass:wasserstein_reg}-(3) so
        \begin{equation*}
            \left|\int c(s,u_1)\,[\mathbb{P}^{b}(ds_{t}\in\cdot\mid h_t)
        -\mathbb{P}^{b^{*}}(ds_{t}\in\cdot\mid h_t)]\right|
        \le K_c\,W_1(\mathbb{P}^{b^*}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h),\,
            \mathbb{P}^{b_0^-}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h)).
        \end{equation*}
        and $r(\cdot ,u_{1})$ is
        $K_{r}$-Lipschitz in $W_{1}$ by Assumption~\ref{ass:wasserstein_reg}-(4) so
        \begin{equation*}
            \text{(I)}\le(K_c+K_{r})\,
            W_1\!\bigl(\mathbb{P}^{b^*}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h),\,
            \mathbb{P}^{b_0^-}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h)\bigr).
        \end{equation*}
        Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:observation_wasserstein} to bound
        $\lVert\mathbb{P}^{b^*}(Y_{t+1}\in\cdot\mid h,u_1)
        -\mathbb{P}^{b_0^-}(Y_{t+1}\in\cdot\mid h,u_1) \rVert_{TV}$:
        \begin{equation*}
            \text{(II)}\le\beta\lVert J^N_\beta\rVert_\infty
            \cdot\alpha^{*}\,
            W_1\!\bigl(\mathbb{P}^{b^*}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h),\,
            \mathbb{P}^{b_0^-}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h)\bigr).
        \end{equation*}
        Taking the maximum over $u_1$,
        \begin{align*}
            &\bigl|\tilde{J}^N_\beta(I_0)-J^*_\beta(I_0)\bigr|\\
            &\le\bigl(\!K_c\!+\!K_{r}\!
            +\!\beta\alpha^{*}\lVert J^N_\beta\rVert_\infty\bigr)
            W_1(\mathbb{P}^{b^*}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h),\,
            \mathbb{P}^{b_0^-}(S_t\in\cdot\mid h))
            \!+\!\beta\!\!\!\sum_{y_2\in \mathbb{Y}}
            \bigl|\tilde{J}^N_\beta(I_1)-J^*_\beta(I_1)\bigr|
            \,\mathbb{P}^{b_0^-}(y_2\mid h,u_1).
        \end{align*}
        Taking expectations, applying $\sup_{\hat{\gamma}}$,
        and iterating yields
        \begin{equation*}
            \mathbb{E}_{b_0^-}\!\bigl[
            \bigl|\tilde{J}^N_\beta(I_0)
            -J^*_\beta(I_0)\bigr|\bigr]
            \le\bigl(K_c+K_{r}
            +\beta\alpha^{*}\lVert J^N_\beta\rVert_\infty\bigr)
            \sum_{t=0}^\infty\beta^t\bar{L}_t^N.
        \end{equation*}
        Substituting
        $\lVert J^N_\beta\rVert_\infty
        \le\frac{\lVert c\rVert_\infty
        +\lVert r\rVert_\infty}{1-\beta}$ concludes the proof.
    \end{proof}

    \begin{theorem}[{\cite[Theorem~2]{demirci2024refined}}]
        \label{thm:wasserstein_policy_bound}
        Under the Assumption~\ref{ass:wasserstein_reg}, for
        $I_0=(b_0^-,h_0^N)$,
        \begin{equation*}
            \mathbb{E}^{\hat{\gamma}}_{b_0^-}\!\left[
            \left|J_\beta(I_0,\gamma^{*,N})
            -J^*_\beta(I_0)\right|
            \,\bigg|\,h_0^N\right]
            \le 2\biggl(K_c+K_{r}
            +\frac{\alpha^{*}\beta
            (\lVert c\rVert_\infty
            +\lVert r\rVert_\infty)}{1-\beta}\biggr)
            \sum_{t=0}^\infty\beta^t\bar{L}_t^N,
        \end{equation*}
        where $\gamma^{*,N}$ is the optimal policy of the approximate
        MDP applied to the original MDP.
    \end{theorem}
    \begin{proof}
        Follows by applying the same argument to
        $|J_\beta(I_0,\gamma^{*,N})-\tilde{J}^N_\beta(I_0)|$
        and combining with Theorem~\ref{thm:wasserstein_approx_bound}
        via the triangle inequality, as in the proof of
        Theorem~\ref{thm:policy_bound}.
    \end{proof}

    As in
    Section~\ref{sec:Approximation Error of the Value Function}, these results 
    are useful only if $\bar{L}_{t}^{N}\to 0$ as $N\to
    \infty$. We establish precisely this for the SLAM model in the next
    section.
